parts.title: Multiple choice (Questions 1–50)
parts.instructions: This paper has 50 multiple-choice questions (1 to 50). Each question has 4 choices. Choose ONE best answer and blacken its letter on the separate answer sheet. Sections: A. Dialogue (1–4), B. Grammar and vocabulary (5–31), C. Word meanings (32–34), D. Table (35–40), E. Reading passage (41–50).

source.notes: Transcribed from the Word source of Version A and checked line by line against the PDF page images (underlined words in Q32–34 marked <u>…</u>; bold words in the stems are plain text). V-B has the same questions in the same order with the options shuffled.
source.printing_note: Printed spellings kept: ‘Asseb’ (Q14), ‘everyday’ (Q31, should be ‘every day’). The story has line numbers 5, 10, 15 in the margin; they are shown as [line 5] etc. in the passage.

exam.answer_key_note: No official key. Answers solved and checked against the Eritrean MoE Grade 6–8 textbooks.

passages.title: Dialogue between a father and his daughter
passages.instructions: Complete the dialogue between a father and his daughter. Choose the father’s correct answers from the choices given (A–D).
paragraphs: Daughter: Where have you been, father?
Daughter: What have you bought for me?
Daughter: From now on I’ll study hard, father.
Choices given: A. Then, I’ll buy you what you want.  B. I went shopping.  C. Nothing.  D. You’re not studying well.

passages.title: Table: where they live, colour, language
passages.instructions: Answer questions 35–40 according to the information in the table.
paragraphs: Name | Place he/she lives in | Colour he/she likes | Language he/she speaks

passages.title: The lion, the fox and the wolf
passages.instructions: Read the story and answer the questions (41–50) according to the information in the story.
paragraphs: Long time ago a very old lion was sick and was lying under a big tree in his forest. All the animals of the forest, except the fox, came to ask how he was. The wolf thought this was a good opportunity to punish the fox for the bad things he did to him. The wolf decided to tell the lion that the fox was not there. He said, [line 5] “You see, mighty King, we have all come to see how you are, except the fox, who hasn’t come near you. He doesn’t care whether you are well or ill.” Just then the fox came in and heard the last words of the wolf. The lion roared at him angrily. The fox begged the lion to be allowed to explain the reason for his absence and said, “Not one of them cares for you as much as I do, oh mighty [line 10] King. I have been going round all the time to many doctors, trying to find some medicine for your illness.” Then the lion said, “So may I ask if you have found one?” The fox answered, “Yes, I have, oh mighty King. One doctor told me that you must kill a wolf, remove his skin and wrap yourself in the skin while it is still warm.”

[line 15] Then the lion turned to the wolf and struck him dead with one blow of his huge hand, so that he could try what the fox told him to do. The fox laughed and said to himself, “That is what comes as the result of doing something bad to others.”
passages.note: Line numbers as printed in the margin: line 5 starts “You see…”, line 10 starts “King.”, line 15 starts “Then the lion…”. Bold in the paper: opportunity (line 3), begged (line 8), them (line 9), he (line 16).

questions.stem: Dialogue, gap (1). Daughter: “Where have you been, father?” Father: “______”

options.A: Then, I’ll buy you what you want.

explanation_steps: The daughter asks WHERE her father has been.
The answer must tell a place or an activity: “I went shopping.”
The next line (“What have you bought for me?”) also shows that he went shopping.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 1 (p. 1–21): conversations.
questions.explain_simple: She asks “Where have you been?”. He says “I went shopping.”
tips: Read the line after the gap too. It often gives a clue.

similar_questions.stem: Mother: Where have you been, Selam?  Selam: ______  Mother: Did you borrow a book?
explanation_steps: “Where” asks for a place. The library also fits the next line about a book.

textbook_ref.rule: In a dialogue, the answer must fit the question before it AND the line after it.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 1 (p. 1–21): conversations

questions.stem: Dialogue, gap (2). Daughter: “What have you bought for me?” Father: “______” Daughter: “But why, father?”

options.A: Then, I’ll buy you what you want.

explanation_steps: The daughter asks what he bought for her.
Then she asks “But why, father?”. People ask “Why?” like this when they are surprised or sad.
So the father bought her nothing: “Nothing.”
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 1 (p. 1–21): conversations.
questions.explain_simple: She says “But why?”. So he bought her nothing.
tips: “But why?” shows the answer before it was a surprise or bad news.

similar_questions.stem: Son: Did you bring me a present?  Father: ______  Son: Oh no! Why not?
explanation_steps: “Oh no! Why not?” shows the answer was “No”.

textbook_ref.rule: In a dialogue, the answer must fit the question before it AND the line after it.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 1 (p. 1–21): conversations

questions.stem: Dialogue, gap (3). Daughter: “But why, father?” Father: “______” Daughter: “From now on I’ll study hard, father.”

options.A: Then, I’ll buy you what you want.

explanation_steps: The father must give a reason: why did he buy nothing?
The next line is “From now on I’ll study hard.” So the reason is about studying.
Answer: “You’re not studying well.”
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 1 (p. 1–21): conversations.
questions.explain_simple: He gives the reason: she does not study well. Then she promises to study hard.
tips: A “why” question needs a reason in the answer.

similar_questions.stem: Pupil: Why can’t I play football today?  Teacher: ______  Pupil: I’ll do it now, teacher.
explanation_steps: The pupil says “I’ll do it now”, so the reason is the homework.

textbook_ref.rule: In a dialogue, the answer must fit the question before it AND the line after it.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 1 (p. 1–21): conversations

questions.stem: Dialogue, gap (4). Daughter: “From now on I’ll study hard, father.” Father: “______”

options.A: Then, I’ll buy you what you want.

explanation_steps: The daughter makes a promise: she will study hard.
The father answers with a promise too: “Then, I’ll buy you what you want.”
“Then” here means “if you do that”.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 1 (p. 1–21): conversations.
questions.explain_simple: She promises to study. He promises to buy her what she wants.
tips: Match each reply to the line just before it.

similar_questions.stem: Son: I will help you in the garden every day.  Mother: ______

options.A: Then, I’ll cook your favourite food.

explanation_steps: The son makes a promise; the mother gives a reward. “Then” means “if you do that”.

textbook_ref.rule: In a dialogue, the answer must fit the question before it AND the line after it.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 1 (p. 1–21): conversations

questions.stem: His brother often ______ films.
explanation_steps: “Often” shows a habit, so we use the present simple.
The subject “his brother” is he (one person), so the verb takes -es: watches.
“is watch” and “watching” alone are wrong forms.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 57; English Grade 8, p. 7.
questions.explain_simple: “Often” = a habit. He/she/it + verb-s: he watches.
tips: He, she, it in the present simple: add -s or -es to the verb.

similar_questions.stem: My sister usually ______ to school by bus.
explanation_steps: “Usually” = habit; my sister = she → goes.

textbook_ref.rule: Present simple: he/she/it takes -s (he watches); questions and negatives use do/does + base verb (Does he help?).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 57; English Grade 8, p. 7

additional_textbook_refs.rule: A singular subject takes a singular verb (is, has, goes); a plural subject takes a plural verb (are, have, go).

questions.stem: ______ he help his mother at home?
explanation_steps: This is a present simple question with the base verb “help”.
With he/she/it we use “Does”: Does he help …?
“Do/Don’t” go with I, you, we, they. “Done” is a past participle.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 57; English Grade 8, p. 7.
questions.explain_simple: With “he” we ask with “Does”: Does he help?
tips: Question with he/she/it in the present: Does + subject + base verb.

similar_questions.stem: ______ your father work in Massawa?
explanation_steps: Your father = he → Does … work?

textbook_ref.rule: Present simple: he/she/it takes -s (he watches); questions and negatives use do/does + base verb (Does he help?).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 57; English Grade 8, p. 7

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb (Why did you travel?). Short answers repeat the auxiliary: Yes, you can.

questions.stem: Did your friend ______ yesterday?
explanation_steps: After “did” we always use the base verb (no -ed, no -ing).
So: Did your friend call yesterday?
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 72; English Grade 8, p. 7.
questions.explain_simple: After “did”, use the simple verb: call.
tips: did + base verb (Did he go? Did she eat?).

similar_questions.stem: Did they ______ the match last night?
explanation_steps: did + base verb → watch.

textbook_ref.rule: Past simple: verb-ed or irregular past form; questions and negatives use did + base verb (Did he call?).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 72; English Grade 8, p. 7

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb (Why did you travel?). Short answers repeat the auxiliary: Yes, you can.

questions.stem: Where is father? I can’t see ______.
explanation_steps: “Father” is a man, one person.
After the verb “see” we need an object pronoun: him (man), her (woman), them (many).
So: I can’t see him.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 61; English Grade 7, p. 7–8.
questions.explain_simple: Father is a man. So we say “him”.
tips: he → him, she → her, they → them after a verb.

similar_questions.stem: Where is your mother? I want to talk to ______.
explanation_steps: Mother = a woman; after “to” use the object pronoun “her”.

textbook_ref.rule: Use an object pronoun (me, him, her, us, them) after a verb or preposition; possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) replace a noun.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 61; English Grade 7, p. 7–8

questions.stem: There are ______ books on the table.
explanation_steps: “There are” goes with a plural noun: books.
“some books” is correct, and “three books” is correct.
“a books” is wrong because “a” goes with one thing only. So the answer is “A and C”.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 148, 274–276; English Grade 8, Units 6–7.
questions.explain_simple: “Some books” and “three books” are both right. “A books” is wrong.
tips: Check every option in the gap. “A and C” can be the answer when both work.

similar_questions.stem: I have ______ oranges in my bag.
explanation_steps: “some oranges” and “two oranges” are both right; “an oranges” is wrong.

textbook_ref.topic: Quantity words (some, any, much, many, too, enough)
textbook_ref.rule: some = an amount with plural or uncountable nouns; too = more than is good; very = a lot; enough = as much as needed.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 148, 274–276; English Grade 8, Units 6–7

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Use 'the' for a thing that is the only one (the moon, the sun) or already known; a/an for one thing that is not specific.
additional_textbook_refs.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 74; English Grade 8, p. 56–58, 204

questions.stem: Senait is the ______ student in our class.
explanation_steps: “the … in our class” compares one student with all the others: we need the superlative.
“Intelligent” is a long word, so we say “the most intelligent”, not “intelligentest”.
“more intelligent” is the comparative (for two things, with “than”).
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 58; English Grade 7, p. 16, 124; English Grade 8, p. 109.
questions.explain_simple: One student compared with the whole class: the most intelligent.
tips: the + most + long adjective + in the class/group.

similar_questions.stem: Asmara is the ______ city in Eritrea.
explanation_steps: Short adjective: the biggest.

textbook_ref.rule: Long adjectives: more ... than / the most ...; short adjectives: -er than / the -est. 'not as ... as' means 'less ... than'.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 58; English Grade 7, p. 16, 124; English Grade 8, p. 109

questions.stem: “Can I come with you?” The correct answer is:
explanation_steps: The question is “Can I …?”. The answer uses the other person: “you can”.
“Yes” goes with “can”; “No” goes with “can’t”.
So “Yes, you can.” is correct. “No, you can” mixes no and yes.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 100–101.
questions.explain_simple: “Can I …?” → “Yes, you can.” or “No, you can’t.”
tips: Short answers: Yes + can, No + can’t. I in the question → you in the answer.

similar_questions.stem: “Can we sit here?” The correct answer is:
explanation_steps: Can we …? → Yes, you can.

textbook_ref.rule: Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb (Why did you travel?). Short answers repeat the auxiliary: Yes, you can.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 100–101

additional_textbook_refs.topic: Modals (must, should, have to, can, may, might)
additional_textbook_refs.rule: Modal verbs (must, should, can, may, might, will) are followed by the base verb without 'to'; have to / ought to keep 'to'.
additional_textbook_refs.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 167–168, 187; English Grade 8, Unit 3 (p. 46–71)

questions.stem: Kemal is riding a bicycle. What is the correct question for this sentence?
explanation_steps: The whole sentence is printed in bold, so any part of it can be the answer.
“Who is riding a bicycle?” → Kemal. “What is Kemal riding?” → a bicycle. “What is Kemal doing?” → He is riding a bicycle.
All three questions are correct questions for this sentence. Answer: D.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 100–101.
questions.explain_simple: The sentence answers all three questions. So all are correct.
tips: Ask yourself: does the sentence answer this question?

similar_questions.stem: Aster is reading a book. Which question does this sentence answer?
explanation_steps: Aster (who), a book (what), reading a book (doing) – it answers all three.

textbook_ref.rule: Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb (Why did you travel?). Short answers repeat the auxiliary: Yes, you can.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 100–101

questions.review_flag: Only the whole sentence is in bold (no single word marked), so D “All are correct” is taken as the intended answer; if one part had been meant, the item would have no single answer. Teacher check.

questions.stem: I can’t hear you. It is ______ noisy.
explanation_steps: “too” means “more than is good”, and it gives a bad result: I can’t hear you.
“noisy enough” would go after the adjective, and “loud noisy” is wrong.
“very noisy” is also possible English, but “too” fits best because of the result (I can’t hear).
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 148, 274–276; English Grade 8, Units 6–7.
questions.explain_simple: It is so noisy that I can’t hear. We say “too noisy”.
tips: too + adjective = more than is good, often with a bad result.

similar_questions.stem: This tea is ______ hot. I can’t drink it.
explanation_steps: The tea is more hot than is good, so I can’t drink it → too hot.

textbook_ref.topic: Quantity words (some, any, much, many, too, enough)
textbook_ref.rule: some = an amount with plural or uncountable nouns; too = more than is good; very = a lot; enough = as much as needed.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 148, 274–276; English Grade 8, Units 6–7

questions.review_flag: “very noisy” (A) is also grammatical; B “too” is the best answer because of the result “I can’t hear you” (textbook G6 p. 274–276 contrasts very/too/enough).

questions.stem: They went to Asseb ______ car.
explanation_steps: For transport without “a/the/my” we use “by”: by car, by bus, by plane.
We say “in a car / in my car”, but here there is no article, so “by car”.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 12; English Grade 8, p. 31, 181.
questions.explain_simple: We travel by car, by bus, by plane.
tips: by + transport (no a/the): by car, by train, by ship.

similar_questions.stem: We usually go to Massawa ______ bus.
explanation_steps: by + transport → by bus.

textbook_ref.rule: Travel: by car/bus/plane; time: at 5 o'clock, on Monday, in June; place: in, on, under, between, next to.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 12; English Grade 8, p. 31, 181

questions.stem: One plus one is ______ two.
explanation_steps: 1 + 1 = 2 is always true. We are 100% sure.
“definitely” means “100% sure”.
“maybe” and “perhaps” mean “not sure”. “can” is a verb and does not fit.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 56, 60–61; English Grade 8, p. 52.
questions.explain_simple: 1 + 1 = 2 is always true. So it is “definitely” two.
tips: definitely = sure; probably = nearly sure; maybe/perhaps = not sure.

similar_questions.stem: The sun ______ rises in the east.
explanation_steps: It is always true → definitely.

textbook_ref.rule: Adverbs of certainty: definitely = 100% sure; probably = nearly sure; maybe/perhaps = not sure.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 56, 60–61; English Grade 8, p. 52

questions.stem: Zahra likes ______ moon. She likes it when it is full.
explanation_steps: There is only one moon, so we say “the moon”.
We also say the sun, the sky, the earth.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 74; English Grade 8, p. 56–58, 204.
questions.explain_simple: There is only one moon. So we say “the moon”.
tips: Use “the” for things there is only one of: the sun, the moon.

similar_questions.stem: ______ sun is very hot today.
explanation_steps: Only one sun → the sun.

textbook_ref.rule: Use 'the' for a thing that is the only one (the moon, the sun) or already known; a/an for one thing that is not specific.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 74; English Grade 8, p. 56–58, 204

questions.stem: Which word has the wrong prefix un?
explanation_steps: unhappy, unclean and unmarried are real words.
The opposite of “correct” is “incorrect”, not “uncorrect”.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 191–192, 199, 232–234.
questions.explain_simple: We say “incorrect”, not “uncorrect”.
tips: Learn the prefix with the word: in-correct, un-happy, dis-like, im-possible.

similar_questions.stem: Which word has the wrong prefix?
explanation_steps: The right word is “impossible”.

textbook_ref.rule: un-, dis-, in-, im-, il-, ir- mean 'not'; each word takes its own prefix (incorrect, not 'uncorrect').
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 191–192, 199, 232–234

questions.stem: In which order would these words be written in a dictionary?
explanation_steps: All the words start with “l”, so look at the second letter: lay (a), leave (e), lie (i), live (i).
lie and live both have “li”; the third letter decides: lie (e) comes before live (v).
Order: lay, leave, lie, live.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 32, 41; English Grade 8, p. 101.
questions.explain_simple: a comes before e, and e before i. So: lay, leave, lie, live.
tips: Same first letter? Look at the second letter, then the third.

similar_questions.stem: Put these words in dictionary order: sun, sad, sit, see
explanation_steps: Second letters: a, e, i, u → sad, see, sit, sun.

textbook_ref.rule: Dictionary order: compare the first letters; if they are the same, compare the second letters, and so on.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 32, 41; English Grade 8, p. 101

questions.stem: Question: ______  Answer: We wanted to see the different trees and animals.

options.A: How did you travel to Filfil Selemuna?
options.B: When did you travel to Filfil Selemuna?
options.C: Why did you travel to Filfil Selemuna?
options.D: Where did you travel to Filfil Selemuna?

explanation_steps: The answer gives a reason: “We wanted to see …”.
A reason answers the question “Why?”.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 100–101.
questions.explain_simple: The answer gives a reason. We ask for a reason with “Why”.
tips: How = way, When = time, Where = place, Why = reason.

similar_questions.stem: Question: ______  Answer: Because I was sick.
explanation_steps: “Because …” gives a reason → Why.

textbook_ref.rule: Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb (Why did you travel?). Short answers repeat the auxiliary: Yes, you can.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 100–101

questions.stem: What was the woman doing in the garden?
explanation_steps: The question uses the past continuous: “was … doing”.
The answer must use the same tense: was + verb-ing → She was planting flowers.
“was plant” is wrong; A and B are other tenses.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 175–176.
questions.explain_simple: “Was … doing?” → “She was planting.”
tips: Answer in the same tense as the question.

similar_questions.stem: What were the boys doing at 5 o’clock?
explanation_steps: were … doing → were playing.

textbook_ref.rule: Past continuous = was/were + verb-ing; it shows an action that was going on at a time in the past.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 175–176

questions.stem: Which word is spelt wrongly?
explanation_steps: connect, excuse and arrest are spelt correctly.
The correct spelling is “justice” (with -ce).
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 72–95 (spelling: doubling letters, dropping 'e').
questions.explain_simple: The right spelling is “justice”.
tips: Many nouns end in -ce: justice, office, police, practice.

similar_questions.stem: Which word is spelt wrongly?
explanation_steps: The right spelling is “notice”.

textbook_ref.rule: Learn the spelling of common words; the sound /s/ at the end of a word is often spelt -ce (justice, office).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 72–95 (spelling: doubling letters, dropping 'e')

questions.stem: My mother is not as short as my father. This is similar to:

options.A: My father is taller than my mother.
options.B: My mother is taller than my father.
options.C: My mother is shorter than my father.
options.D: They are of the same height.

explanation_steps: “not as short as” means “less short”, so the mother is taller.
So: My mother is taller than my father.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 58; English Grade 7, p. 16, 124; English Grade 8, p. 109.
questions.explain_simple: Mother is not as short as father. So mother is taller.
tips: not as + adjective + as = the opposite comparison (not as short as = taller than).

similar_questions.stem: Ali is not as old as Omar. This means:
explanation_steps: Ali is less old → Omar is older.

textbook_ref.rule: Long adjectives: more ... than / the most ...; short adjectives: -er than / the -est. 'not as ... as' means 'less ... than'.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 58; English Grade 7, p. 16, 124; English Grade 8, p. 109

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Check who does what, the tense and the comparison; the new sentence must say exactly the same thing.
additional_textbook_refs.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 16 (comparison); English Grade 8, p. 105 (be able to)

questions.stem: How many cars ______ each day?
explanation_steps: Cars do not sell; people sell cars. So we need the passive.
“each day” = present; cars = plural → are + past participle: are sold.
“are sell” and “were sell” are wrong forms.
Textbook: English Grade 6, p. 134; English Grade 7, p. 145; English Grade 8, p. 12.
questions.explain_simple: Cars are sold by people. Passive: are + sold.
tips: Passive = am/is/are + past participle (sold, made, built).

similar_questions.stem: How many books ______ every year in this school?
explanation_steps: Books are used (by people) → passive: are used.

textbook_ref.rule: Passive = am/is/are/was/were + past participle (Cars are sold). Use it when the doer is not important.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 6, p. 134; English Grade 7, p. 145; English Grade 8, p. 12

questions.stem: Semere: Can I borrow your bicycle, please?  Osman: I’m sorry, Dawit ______ it.
explanation_steps: A past action with a result now (the bicycle is not here) → present perfect.
Dawit = he → has + past participle: has taken.
“taked” is not a word; “have” goes with I/you/we/they.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 150; English Grade 8, p. 42, 157.
questions.explain_simple: Dawit (he) + has taken. The bicycle is not here now.
tips: Present perfect: he/she/it has + past participle.

similar_questions.stem: I can’t find my pen. Someone ______ it.
explanation_steps: Someone = one person → has taken.

textbook_ref.rule: Present perfect = have/has + past participle (he has taken). Use has with he/she/it and one person.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 150; English Grade 8, p. 42, 157

questions.stem: If he is angry, he ______.
explanation_steps: If + present simple, will + base verb (first conditional): If he is angry, he will cry.
The zero conditional (If + present, present) is also correct for a habit: If he is angry, he cries.
“crying” and “to cry” are wrong.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 161; English Grade 8, p. 34, 129.
questions.explain_simple: If he is angry, he will cry. (“he cries” is also right.)
tips: If + present, … will + verb.

similar_questions.stem: If it rains tomorrow, we ______ at home.
explanation_steps: tomorrow = one future event → first conditional: will stay.

textbook_ref.rule: First conditional: If + present simple, will + base verb. Zero conditional (always true): If + present, present. Second: If + past, would + base verb.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 161; English Grade 8, p. 34, 129

questions.review_flag: Two defensible answers: A “will cry” (first conditional) and C “cries” (zero conditional, a habit) – both are taught in English Grade 8, p. 34. A is taken as the intended answer; both accepted.

questions.stem: I am able to finish reading the book on time. This is similar to:

options.A: I can finish reading the book on time.
options.D: I must finish reading the book on time.

explanation_steps: “be able to” means the same as “can” (ability).
So “I am able to finish” = “I can finish”.
“must” shows necessity, not ability.
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 105.
questions.explain_simple: “Am able to” means “can”.
tips: be able to = can; was able to = could.

similar_questions.stem: She is able to swim. This means:
explanation_steps: is able to = can.

textbook_ref.rule: 'be able to' means the same as 'can' (ability).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 105

additional_textbook_refs.rule: Check who does what, the tense and the comparison; the new sentence must say exactly the same thing.
additional_textbook_refs.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 16 (comparison); English Grade 8, p. 105 (be able to)

questions.stem: You and your brother must clean ______.
explanation_steps: The subject is “you and your brother” = you (plural).
The reflexive pronoun for plural “you” is “yourselves”.
“ourself” is not a word; “themselves” is for “they”.
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 56, 112.
questions.explain_simple: You + your brother = you (two people) → yourselves.
tips: you (one) → yourself; you (many) → yourselves.

similar_questions.stem: Senait and I made this cake ______.
explanation_steps: Senait and I = we → ourselves.

textbook_ref.rule: Reflexive pronouns show that the subject and the object are the same person: you (plural) → yourselves.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 56, 112

questions.stem: Our teacher said, “I am sick.” The correct indirect speech is:

options.A: Our teacher said that he is sick.
options.B: Our teacher said that I was sick.
options.C: Our teacher said that I am sick.
options.D: Our teacher said that he was sick.

explanation_steps: In indirect speech, “I” changes to “he” (the teacher).
After “said”, the present “am” moves back to the past “was”.
So: Our teacher said that he was sick.
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 151, 174–175.
questions.explain_simple: “I” becomes “he”, and “am” becomes “was”.
tips: Reported speech: change the person, and move the tense back (am → was).

similar_questions.stem: Saba said, “I am tired.” Indirect speech:

options.A: Saba said that she was tired.
options.B: Saba said that I am tired.
options.C: Saba said that she is tire.

explanation_steps: I → she, am → was.

textbook_ref.rule: In reported speech after 'said', change the pronoun (I → he/she) and move the tense back (am → was, will → would).
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 151, 174–175

questions.stem: I like ______ the cows.
explanation_steps: After “like” we use verb-ing (or to + base verb).
“milking” is correct. “to milking” mixes the two forms and is wrong.
“I like milk the cows” and “I like milked” are wrong.
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 13–14.
questions.explain_simple: After “like”, use verb-ing: I like milking.
tips: like + verb-ing, or like + to + verb. Never “to + verb-ing”.

similar_questions.stem: My brother likes ______ football.
explanation_steps: like + verb-ing → playing.

textbook_ref.rule: After like/love/enjoy/finish we can use verb-ing; after want/decide/hope we use to + verb. Never 'to + verb-ing'.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 13–14

questions.stem: Students ______ obey their parents.
explanation_steps: The sentence talks about a duty, so we need “must” or “have to”.
“must to” is wrong: after “must” there is no “to”.
So “have to” is correct: Students have to obey their parents.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 167–168, 187; English Grade 8, Unit 3 (p. 46–71).
questions.explain_simple: It is a duty. We say “have to obey” (never “must to”).
tips: must + verb (no to); have to + verb.

similar_questions.stem: You ______ wear a uniform at school.
explanation_steps: you + have to; “must to” and “can to” are wrong.

textbook_ref.topic: Modals (must, should, have to, can, may, might)
textbook_ref.rule: Modal verbs (must, should, can, may, might, will) are followed by the base verb without 'to'; have to / ought to keep 'to'.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 167–168, 187; English Grade 8, Unit 3 (p. 46–71)

questions.stem: They eat fruit everyday ______ they become healthy.
explanation_steps: Why do they eat fruit? To become healthy. This is a purpose.
“so that” introduces a purpose.
“because” gives a reason, “but” shows a contrast, “because of” needs a noun.
Textbook: English Grade 8, p. 30, 68, 82, 98–99.
questions.explain_simple: They eat fruit to be healthy. Purpose → so that.
tips: so that = in order to (purpose).

similar_questions.stem: She studies hard ______ she can pass the exam.
explanation_steps: Purpose → so that.

textbook_ref.rule: because + reason; so that + purpose; but/however + contrast; and + addition; so + result.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, p. 30, 68, 82, 98–99

questions.review_flag: Minor misprint: ‘everyday’ should be ‘every day’ (two words) here. It does not change the answer.

questions.stem: The wind was very strong and it <u>destroyed</u> a lot of houses and crops. Therefore, many people do not have houses and food at this time.
explanation_steps: After the wind, people have no houses and no food.
So the wind damaged the houses and crops very badly: destroy = to damage badly.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227.
questions.explain_simple: People lost their houses. So “destroy” means “to damage badly”.
tips: Read the next sentence: it often explains the new word.

similar_questions.stem: The fire <u>destroyed</u> the old school. Now the children learn under a tree. ‘Destroyed’ means:
explanation_steps: The school cannot be used, so it was badly damaged.

textbook_ref.rule: Read the whole sentence: the words before and after tell you the meaning of the new word.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227

questions.stem: The cat was hungry. So, it <u>chased</u> the rat up to the hole. But it couldn’t catch the rat.
explanation_steps: The cat wanted to catch the rat and ran after it “up to the hole”.
It did not catch it, so it did not eat it.
chase = to follow quickly to catch.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227.
questions.explain_simple: The cat ran after the rat. “Chase” means to follow quickly.
tips: Check the options against the whole story: the cat couldn’t catch the rat, so it didn’t eat it.

similar_questions.stem: The dog <u>chased</u> the boy, but the boy ran into the house. ‘Chased’ means:
explanation_steps: The dog ran after him to catch him.

textbook_ref.rule: Read the whole sentence: the words before and after tell you the meaning of the new word.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227

questions.stem: Ali: “Mother, I’m sorry that I came late. Are you <u>upset</u> with me?”  Mother: “Yes, I’m really upset with you. I don’t want to talk to you.”
explanation_steps: Ali came late and says sorry.
The mother does not want to talk to him, so she is angry.
upset = feeling angry or unhappy.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227.
questions.explain_simple: The mother does not want to talk to him. She is angry (upset).
tips: Feelings words: look at what the person says or does.

similar_questions.stem: Hana was <u>upset</u> because her friend broke her pen. ‘Upset’ means:
explanation_steps: Losing a pen makes her angry/unhappy.

textbook_ref.rule: Read the whole sentence: the words before and after tell you the meaning of the new word.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227

questions.stem: ______ and ______ live in a place where we can see many cars.
explanation_steps: We see many cars in a town.
In the table, Nahom and Humed live in a town.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: Many cars are in towns. Nahom and Humed live in a town.
tips: Change the words: “a place with many cars” = a town.

similar_questions.stem: Who lives in a place with farms and animals? (same table)
explanation_steps: Farms are in villages: Zeineb and Michael.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

questions.stem: If you want to speak to Humed, you should know ______ language.
explanation_steps: Find Humed’s row, then the “Language” column: Nara.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: Humed speaks Nara.
tips: Find the row first, then the column.

similar_questions.stem: Michael speaks ______ (same table).
explanation_steps: Michael’s row: Bilen.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

questions.stem: Who are more likely to be farmers?
explanation_steps: Farmers usually live in villages.
Zeineb and Michael live in a village.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: Farmers live in villages. Zeineb and Michael live in a village.
tips: “More likely” = use what you know about life plus the table.

similar_questions.stem: Who are more likely to go to a big market with shops and cars every day?
explanation_steps: Town people: Nahom and Humed.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

additional_textbook_refs.rule: A 'true' statement must agree with the text in every part; the text may say it in other words.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false?

options.A: All of the people speak different languages.
options.B: Two people like the same colour.
options.C: None of the people lives in a town.

explanation_steps: A: Tigrigna, Saho, Bilen, Nara – all different. True.
B: Zeineb and Humed both like green. True.
C: Nahom and Humed live in a town. So C is false.
D says A and B are false, but they are true.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: Two people live in a town. So “None lives in a town” is false.
tips: For “false” questions, test each sentence; the wrong one is the answer.

similar_questions.stem: Which is false? (same table)
explanation_steps: Michael lives in a village.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

questions.stem: ______ lives in a town but doesn’t speak Tigrigna?
explanation_steps: Town: Nahom and Humed.
Nahom speaks Tigrigna, Humed speaks Nara. So: Humed.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: Humed lives in a town and speaks Nara, not Tigrigna.
tips: Check both parts of the question.

similar_questions.stem: Who lives in a village but doesn’t like green? (same table)
explanation_steps: Village: Zeineb (green), Michael (yellow) → Michael.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

questions.review_flag: The stem is a statement with a gap but ends with a question mark (printing). It does not change the answer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?

options.A: Two people live in different places but like the same colour.
options.B: Two people like the same colour and both live in villages.
options.C: Two people like the same colour and speak the same language.

explanation_steps: Zeineb (village) and Humed (town) both like green: different places, same colour → A is true.
B: the two green people do not both live in villages. False.
C: they speak Saho and Nara. False. So D is false too.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data.
questions.explain_simple: Zeineb and Humed both like green, but one lives in a village and one in a town.
tips: Check every part of the sentence with the table.

similar_questions.stem: Which is true? (same table)

options.A: Two people live in a town and like red.
options.B: Two people live in a village.

explanation_steps: Zeineb and Michael live in a village.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the right row (person/thing) and the right column (fact); check every part of a statement before you call it true.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 6 (p. 120–141): graphs and data

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?

options.A: The fox came before all the other animals.
options.B: The fox did not come at all to see the lion.
options.C: The wolf and the fox were true friends.
options.D: The fox heard what the wolf told the lion about him.

explanation_steps: “Just then the fox came in and heard the last words of the wolf.” So D is true.
The fox came last, not first (A), and he did come (B). The wolf wanted to punish him, so they were not friends (C).
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories).
questions.explain_simple: The story says the fox came in and heard the wolf’s words.
tips: Find the sentence in the story that matches the option.

similar_questions.stem: According to the story, the lion was:
explanation_steps: “a very old lion was sick”.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the part of the text with the same words as the question; read that sentence carefully.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories)

questions.stem: What does the word “opportunity” (line 3) mean?
explanation_steps: The wolf saw the fox was absent. He thought it was a good chance to punish the fox.
opportunity = chance.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227.
questions.explain_simple: “A good opportunity” = a good chance.
tips: Put each option in the sentence: “a good chance to punish the fox” makes sense.

similar_questions.stem: “I had the opportunity to visit Keren.” ‘Opportunity’ means:
explanation_steps: opportunity = chance.

textbook_ref.rule: Put each option in place of the word; the one that keeps the meaning of the sentence is correct.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227

questions.stem: The word “them” (line 9) refers to:

options.A: the fox and the wolf but not the others
options.B: the lion and all other animals
options.C: the lion and the wolf but not the others
options.D: all other animals except the fox and the lion

explanation_steps: The fox says to the lion: “Not one of them cares for you as much as I do.”
“you” is the lion and “I” is the fox.
So “them” means all the other animals (not the fox, not the lion).
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 7–8 (pronouns).
questions.explain_simple: The fox talks about the other animals. “Them” = the other animals.
tips: “you” and “I” in the same sentence cannot be “them”.

similar_questions.stem: “The children came to the party. All of them were happy.” ‘Them’ refers to:
explanation_steps: them = the children.

textbook_ref.topic: Reference words (he, she, it, them, this)
textbook_ref.rule: A pronoun (he, it, them, this) stands for a noun that came before it; read the sentences before it.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 7–8 (pronouns)

questions.stem: “Not one of them cares for you as much as I do, oh mighty King …” Who said this?
explanation_steps: “The fox begged the lion … and said, ‘Not one of them cares for you …’.”
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories).
questions.explain_simple: The fox said it to the lion.
tips: Look for “said” just before the quotation marks.

similar_questions.stem: Who said, “So may I ask if you have found one?”
explanation_steps: “Then the lion said, ‘So may I ask …’”.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the part of the text with the same words as the question; read that sentence carefully.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories)

questions.stem: What does the word “begged” (line 8) mean?
explanation_steps: The lion was angry with the fox. The fox was afraid, and he asked the lion strongly to let him explain.
beg = to ask for something in a worried, strong way. Answer: “asked worryingly”.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227.
questions.explain_simple: The fox was worried and asked the lion for a chance to explain.
tips: Think how the person feels: the fox was in danger and worried.

similar_questions.stem: The hungry boy begged for some bread. ‘Begged’ means:
explanation_steps: beg = ask strongly because you need something.

textbook_ref.rule: Put each option in place of the word; the one that keeps the meaning of the sentence is correct.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227

questions.stem: The word “he” (line 16) refers to:
explanation_steps: “The lion … struck him dead … so that he could try what the fox told him to do.”
The lion wanted to try the “medicine” (the wolf’s skin). So “he” = the lion.
Textbook: English Grade 7, p. 7–8 (pronouns).
questions.explain_simple: The lion killed the wolf so that he (the lion) could try the medicine.
tips: Ask: who wanted to do this? Read the whole sentence.

similar_questions.stem: “Ali gave the book to Omar because he had finished reading it.” Who had finished reading it?
explanation_steps: Ali gave the book away because he (Ali) had finished it.

textbook_ref.topic: Reference words (he, she, it, them, this)
textbook_ref.rule: A pronoun (he, it, them, this) stands for a noun that came before it; read the sentences before it.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 7–8 (pronouns)

questions.stem: What would cure the lion according to the fox?

options.B: wrapping himself in a fox’s skin
options.D: wrapping himself in a wolf’s skin

explanation_steps: The fox said: “kill a wolf, remove his skin and wrap yourself in the skin while it is still warm.”
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories).
questions.explain_simple: The fox said: wrap yourself in a wolf’s skin.
tips: Be careful with small differences: wolf/fox, eating/wrapping.

similar_questions.stem: Where was the lion lying?
explanation_steps: “lying under a big tree in his forest”.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the part of the text with the same words as the question; read that sentence carefully.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories)

questions.stem: What happened to the wolf at the end?

options.A: He was asked to leave the forest.
options.B: He was killed by the lion.
options.C: He became a good friend of the lion.

explanation_steps: “The lion turned to the wolf and struck him dead with one blow.” So the lion killed the wolf.
Textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories).
questions.explain_simple: The lion killed the wolf.
tips: “struck him dead” = killed him.

similar_questions.stem: What did the fox do at the end?
explanation_steps: “The fox laughed and said to himself …”.

textbook_ref.rule: Find the part of the text with the same words as the question; read that sentence carefully.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, reading lessons (e.g. Unit 10, p. 199–220: stories)

questions.stem: Which word in the 2nd paragraph has the same meaning as “hit”?
explanation_steps: 2nd paragraph: “… struck him dead with one blow of his huge hand”.
struck is the past of strike = hit.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227.
questions.explain_simple: “Struck” means “hit”.
tips: Look for an action word (verb) when the given word is a verb.

similar_questions.stem: Which word has the same meaning as “very big”?
explanation_steps: huge = very big.

textbook_ref.rule: Put each option in place of the word; the one that keeps the meaning of the sentence is correct.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Appendix 1: Vocabulary list, p. 221–227

additional_textbook_refs.topic: Opposites and words with the same meaning
additional_textbook_refs.rule: A synonym has the same meaning (hit = strike); an opposite has the reverse meaning (happy – sad).
additional_textbook_refs.note: textbook: English Grade 7, p. 222; English Grade 8, p. 160

questions.stem: The best title for the story could be:

options.A: The lion, the fox and the wolf
options.C: The death of the old lion

explanation_steps: The story has three main characters: the lion, the fox and the wolf.
B leaves out the fox, who is very important. C is wrong: the lion does not die.
D is too general. So A is best.
Textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 10 (p. 199–220).
questions.explain_simple: The story is about three animals: the lion, the fox and the wolf.
tips: The best title covers the whole story.

similar_questions.stem: A story tells how a clever girl helps her village find water. The best title is:

options.B: The clever girl and the water

explanation_steps: It covers the main person and the main event.

textbook_ref.rule: The best title covers the whole text, not only one part.
textbook_ref.note: textbook: English Grade 8, Unit 10 (p. 199–220)
